title: Climate change sceptics have lost the plot as Europe burns
gist: Alan Rusbridger uses Allister Heath's Telegraph column urging Britain to 'scrap net zero' and build swimming pools — published as France and Spain burned — to argue climate scepticism on the British right has become self-parody. He notes the Telegraph's own op-ed page is now split, with Tim Stanley and Ambrose Evans-Pritchard arguing the market-led clean-energy transition is happening for economic reasons, while Kemi Badenoch has made repudiating the 2050 net zero target a candidate-selection litmus test.

themes.theme: The Telegraph's internal split on net zero

insights.claim: The Telegraph's op-ed page ran climate columns every day of one week in late July 2026 with two of the five arguing against the paper's traditional climate scepticism, signalling a genuine fracture inside the British right's flagship newspaper.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: A crack in right-wing media consensus on net zero is an early signal that UK anti-green policy risk may be less durable than polling suggests.
insights.quote: These columns, by respected Telegraph writers, will have disorientated many readers, who have been groomed over many years to think the precise opposite.
insights.locator: These columns, by respected Telegraph writers

insights.claim: Ambrose Evans-Pritchard argued Kemi Badenoch risks destroying the Conservative party by turning opposition to net zero into an ideological litmus test rather than embracing the market-led clean-energy revolution.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Frames anti-net-zero positioning as an existential party-management risk, not just a policy stance — watch for Conservative repositioning.
insights.quote: arguing that Kemi Badenoch risks destroying the Conservative party by allowing opposition to net zero to become an ideological litmus test instead of embracing the market-led clean-energy revolution
insights.locator: And on Wednesday Ambrose Evans Pritchard went further

insights.claim: Kemi Badenoch has barred anyone unwilling to repudiate the UK's statutory 2050 net zero target from standing as a Conservative candidate, a screen that has excluded even Grant Shapps.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Hard-coded candidate screening means a Conservative government would face structural pressure to repeal the 2050 statutory target — direct risk to UK renewables and CfD pipelines.
insights.quote: Badenoch has famously decided to ban anyone from being a Conservative candidate if they are unwilling to repudiate the UK’s statutory 2050 net zero target.
insights.locator: Badenoch, evidently stung by Evans Pritchard

insights.claim: Kemi Badenoch publicly characterised net zero as a 'political fiction' in a letter to the Telegraph.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: The Conservative leader's explicit framing removes ambiguity about a future government's climate policy direction.
insights.quote: he described net zero as a “political fiction.”
insights.locator: Badenoch, evidently stung by Evans Pritchard

themes.theme: Adaptation-boosterism as the new sceptic position

insights.claim: The frontier of British climate scepticism has shifted from denying warming to declaring the war already lost and reframing a hotter climate as an economic opportunity, exemplified by Allister Heath's 'We've lost the war against climate change. Time to scrap net zero.'
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Anti-mitigation arguments are migrating to a defeatist-adaptation frame — anticipate policy pushes toward adaptation spending and away from decarbonisation capex.
insights.quote: “We’ve lost the war against climate change. Time to scrap net zero.”
insights.locator: Having consistently argued against doing anything

insights.claim: The claim that hot southern regions like Dubai, Florida, South East Asia and Israel are blossoming economically ignores that Dubai took a year to eighteen months of rainfall in under 24 hours in April 2024, that insurers have withdrawn from parts of Florida or sharply raised premiums over climate losses, and that Israel faces intensifying heatwaves and water stress.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Insurer retreat from Florida is the concrete market price of climate risk — the clearest live evidence that hot-region 'blossoming' narratives fail underwriting tests.
insights.quote: many insurers have withdrawn from parts of the state, or have sharply increased premiums because of mounting climate-related losses
insights.locator: Florida evokes memories of multiple destructive hurricanes

insights.claim: British climate-sceptic rhetoric contains an implicit exceptionalism in which the Channel is imagined to insulate the UK from continental extreme heat, a hedge embedded in the qualifier 'if that is indeed to be our fate'.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: UK-specific climate complacency is a reason domestic adaptation spending lags continental peers, leaving infrastructure exposure underpriced.
insights.quote: Note the sly last clause, which suggests that Britain—perhaps by virtue of the English Channel, which has protected this sceptred isle over so many centuries—may prove to be immune from continental fads like extreme heat.

themes.theme: Clean energy adoption driven by economics, not ideology

insights.claim: Kenya's high proportion of renewable electricity and Pakistan's rapid rooftop solar adoption show clean energy is spreading for practical and economic reasons rather than ideological ones.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Emerging-market solar uptake is a cost-driven trend independent of Western climate politics — supports demand for panels and distributed generation regardless of UK policy.
insights.quote: He cited Kenya’s high proportion of renewable electricity and Pakistan’s rapid adoption of rooftop solar as evidence that clean energy is spreading for practical and economic reasons, not simply ideological ones.
insights.locator: On Monday Tim Stanley penned an elegant critique

insights.claim: Tim Stanley argued the contemporary right has unthinkingly fallen into a pattern of climate scepticism that is itself distinctly unconservative.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: An internal conservative critique gives cover for a future right-wing pivot back toward climate policy.
insights.locator: On Monday Tim Stanley penned an elegant critique

insights.claim: Royal Society fellow Sir Brian Hoskins argues net zero is dictated by the laws of physics rather than being an arbitrary slogan, because halting warming requires net greenhouse gas emissions to stop, and that slowing the transition guarantees escalating climate costs falling hardest on lower-income households.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: Delay does not reduce total cost, it reallocates it to later and to poorer households — a distributional argument that will shape future climate-policy backlash.
insights.quote: Net zero is not an arbitrary slogan, rather it is dictated by the laws of physics. To halt warming, net greenhouse gas emissions must stop.
insights.locator: A sober letter from Sir Brian Hoskins

insights.claim: With uncontrolled wildfires raging outside Bordeaux and Madrid and a wall of flames in France's Gironde region in late July 2026, British sceptics are simultaneously pushing to restart North Sea drilling.
insights.speaker: Alan Rusbridger
insights.so_what: North Sea licensing is the concrete policy fight where UK climate politics translates into oil and gas capex decisions.
insights.quote: as terrifying fires rage beyond control outside Bordeaux and Madrid, the real climate fanatics are clamouring to start drilling again in the North Sea
